results.summary: This design implements a recurrent neural network hidden-state update in which an 8-bit input current is multiplied by an 8x8 weight matrix. The hidden state is reset to zero, and the user changes the input current to observe the resulting output current. The pin names and documentation are largely inherited from the 7-segment demo template, so the actual RNN behavior is only briefly described. It is a minimal demonstration rather than a complete neural network system.

This design computes the Collatz sequence for a large integer and reports the orbit length and the upper 16 bits of the highest value reached. Input bytes are uploaded one at a time into a 144-bit register, and results are read back through an address and select interface. A start pin triggers computation and a busy indicator signals completion. Silicon testing confirmed that the project test cases and additional cases worked as expected.

This is an implementation of the SAP-1 simple-as-possible computer architecture, containing a program counter, registers, adder, memory, instruction register, bus, and controller. It has no external inputs and runs autonomously from the clock, performing only addition and subtraction on 8-bit values. The bus output can currently only be observed with an oscilloscope, and the author suggests adding a 7-segment display controller as an enhancement. The design is based on the well-known Malvino and Brown architecture popularized by Ben Eater.

This design accepts an 8-bit event signal with x, y, p, and t parameters and outputs the signal only when the p bit is high, filtering it to reduce noise. It also includes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal logic driving a 7-segment display, with the lower counter bits exposed on the bidirectional pins. The input pins program a 24-bit compare value that sets the counting rate. The documentation describes the counter behavior in detail but gives only a brief description of the denoising function.

This design counts seconds and displays the value on a 7-segment display, with the lower counter bits also available on the bidirectional pins. The input pins program a 24-bit compare register so the counting rate can be changed from the default one-second interval. It is a standard Tiny Tapeout Verilog demo intended to show clock division and binary-to-decimal conversion. The documentation is complete and describes both the default and programmable counting behavior.

This project is intended to implement a random dropout circuit inspired by the dropout mechanism used to prevent overfitting in neural networks. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test both state only that they are not written yet. The pin names are inherited from the 7-segment counter demo template and do not reflect the described dropout function. There is not enough information to determine the actual implementation or how to use it.

This design implements two leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and a spike-timing dependent plasticity module that updates a synaptic weight based on the timing difference between pre- and post-synaptic spikes. A drive current is applied to the neuron and integrated every clock cycle, with the LIF spike, LIF state, and synaptic weight brought out as outputs. The documentation describes the learning rule and testing procedure at a high level. It is a compact hardware demonstration of a biologically inspired learning mechanism.

This project is described as a silicon chip design of a convolutional neural network, but the how-it-works section only says the explanation will be added later. The how-to-test section is copied from the 7-segment counter demo and does not describe CNN testing. The pin names are also inherited from that demo template and do not indicate CNN-specific interfaces. There is essentially no usable documentation for the actual design.

This is an 8-bit CPU design whose Verilog code was generated by Bing AI. The input pins carry instruction register bits and formula right-side bits, while the outputs drive a 7-segment display. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test are still placeholders, so the instruction set and operation are not described. The design cannot be fully evaluated from the available information.

This design implements the game Tetris in hardware, using VGA outputs for video and buttons for moving and rotating pieces. It requires an external memory connected over the bidirectional pins, which the author implemented on an RP2040 based on existing Teensy code. Silicon testing reported that the design works great. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test are otherwise placeholders.
